THESE WRIT PETITIONS COMING ON FOR HEARING, THIS DAY, THE COURT MADE THE FOLLOWING:
 -3-  WP No. 67426 of 2010  C/W WP No. 64139 of 2010  ORDER

Both these petitions assail the impugned acquisition proceedings in relation to the subject lands of the petitioners which were sought to be acquired by the respondents No.1 to 3 for the benefit of the 4th respondent-APMC pursuant to the impugned preliminary notification dated 21.12.2009 issued under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (for short 'L.A. Act') and the final notification dated 24.05.2010 issued by the respondents.

2. The petitioners in W.P. No. 64139/2010 owned and possessed 2 acres 17 guntas of land in Sy. No.
129/1-K of Muchakandi village, Bagalkot Hobli, Bagalkot Taluk and District and they are the sons of the petitioner in W.P. No. 67426/2010, in whose favour they executed a registered gift deed dated 15.09.2009 to an extent of 32 guntas.

Out of the total extent of 2 acres 17 guntas owned and possessed by the petitioners in both the petitions, the subject matter of the petitions is an extent of 28 guntas of land notified under the impugned notifications.

Since common questions of law and fact arise for consideration in both the petitions, they are taken up together and disposed of by this common order.
3. I have heard learned counsel appearing for the petitioners and the counsel appearing for the respective respondents and perused the material on record.

4. In addition to reiterating the various contentions as urged in the writ petitions, learned counsel for the petitioners submits that the subject land measuring 28 guntas is part and parcel of a total extent of 2 acres 17 guntas in Sy. No. 129/1-K which was converted for non agricultural purposes in favour of the petitioners on 08.06.2001.

On 02.04.2002, the petitioners instituted a suit in O.S. No.
71/2002 on the file of First Addl. Sr. Civil Judge, Bagalkot for possession, injunction, etc. alleging that the 4th respondent- APMC had illegally encroached upon the subject land measuring 28 guntas belonging to the petitioners.

sentences.text: The said suit having been contested by the 4th respondent, the trial Court proceeded to pass judgment and decree dated 18.01.2006 in favour of the petitioners directing the 4th respondent to hand over possession of the subject property to the petitioners.

5. Aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, 4th respondent-APMC preferred an appeal in R.F.A No. 753/2006 before this Court which also dismissed the same vide judgment and decree dated 13.12.2007 confirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court passed in favour Girish S/O Rajshekhar Kanthi vs State Of Karnataka on 14 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/185926136/

sentences.text: Aggrieved by the same, 4th respondent-APMC preferred SLP 5094/2008 which was also dismissed by the Apex Court vide order dated 12.01.2009.

Thereafter, since the 4th respondent-APMC did not comply with the aforesaid orders, petitioners instituted execution proceedings in E.P. No. 10/2008 in which the executing Court appointed a Court Commissioner who demarcated the subject property and handed over possession of the property to the petitioner and submitted a report which was accepted by the executing Court vide order dated 25.04.2009 and the execution proceedings were closed as the decree in favour of the petitioners having been fully satisfied.
Aggrieved by the said order of the executing Court in E.P. No. 10/2008, 4th respondent-APMC preferred CRP No. 1056/2009 before this Court which was also dismissed vide final order dated 13.08.2009.
The aforesaid order passed by the executing Court and confirmed by this Court has attained finality and become conclusive and binding upon the 4th respondent-APMC.

It is the grievance of the petitioner that despite all the aforesaid proceedings which have attained finality and become conclusive in favour of the petitioner, the respondents No.1 to 3 have colluded with each other and fraudulently issued the impugned preliminary notification dated 21.12.2009 under Sec. 4(1) of the L.A. Act illegally purporting to invoke the urgency provisions of Sec. 17 of the L.A. Act thereby dispensing with the mandatory enquiry provided under Sec. 5-A of the L.A. Act and despite the petitioners filing their objections on 01.02.2010 along with all relevant documents including the aforesaid Court proceedings and orders pursuant to which the second respondent addressed a communication dated 04.02.2010 directing the third respondent- LAO to consider the said objections and documents of the petitioners, the respondents have proceeded to issue the impugned final notification dated 24.05.2010 which is an outcome of bad faith, malafides and colourable exercise of power and the same deserves to be quashed.

6. Per contra, learned counsel for the 4th respondent-APMC as well as learned HCGP, in addition to reiterating the various contentions urged in the petition and referring to the material on record submitted that there is no merit in the petition and the same is liable to be dismissed.

7. The undisputed material on record referred to supra, clearly discloses that the impugned acquisition proceedings were initiated after conclusion of the earlier round of litigation between the petitioner and the 4th respondent which ultimately culminated in favour of the petitioner and against the 4th respondent and the same having attained finality and become conclusive was binding upon the 4th respondent.

In this context, a perusal of the preliminary notification dated 21.12.2009 will clearly indicate that the only property sought to be acquired under the said notification was the subject land of the petitioners by invoking Sec. 17 of the L.A. Act and mandatory enquiry under Section 5-A of the L.A. Act was sought to be dispensed with by the respondents;
however, neither the said notification nor any other material placed by the respondents establish the urgency or the exceptional/ extra ordinary circumstances which warranted invocation of the urgency clause contained in Sec.17 thereby dispensing with the mandatory enquiry contemplated u/S 5-A of the L.A. Act; in fact, except for stating that the subject lands were required for the purpose of 4th respondent-APMC, neither valid nor justifiable reasons are assigned either in the preliminary notification nor in any other document by the respondents to justify invocation of Sec.17 and consequently, the very invocation of Sec. 17 by the respondents is illegal and contrary to the law laid down by the Apex Court and this Court in the following judgments, i.e., (i) Hamid Ali Khan Vs. In Hamid Ali Khan (supra) the Apex Court has held as under:
13.
In Narayan Govind Gavate and Others v. State of Maharashtra and Others7, a Bench of 3 learned Judges (1977) 1 SCC 133 was dealing with a notification issued under Section 17(4).

entities.text: Narayan Govind Gavate and Others v. State of Maharashtra and Others7
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The public purpose recited in the notification was development and utilisation of the land as a residential and industrial area.
The lands were described as waste and arable land and urgency provision was invoked resulting in the notification being issued.

This court inter alia held:
"10.

It is true that, in such cases, the formation of an opinion is a subjective matter, as held by this Court repeatedly with regard to situations in which administrative authorities have to form certain opinions before taking actions they are empowered to take.
They are expected to know better the difference between a right or wrong opinion than courts could ordinarily on such matters.
Nevertheless, that opinion has to be based upon some relevant materials in order to pass the test which courts do impose.
That test basically is: Was the authority concerned acting within the scope of its powers or in the sphere where its opinion and discretion must be permitted to have full play?

Once the court comes to the conclusion that the authority concerned was acting within the scope of its powers and had some material, however meagre, on which it could reasonably base its opinion, the courts should not and will not interfere.

There might, however, be cases in which the power is exercised in such an obviously arbitrary or perverse fashion, without regard to the actual and undeniable facts, or, in other words, so unreasonably as to leave no doubt whatsoever in the mind of a court that there has been an excess of power.

There may also be cases where the mind of the authority concerned has not been applied at all, due to misunderstanding of the law or some other reason, to what was legally imperative for it to consider.

24. Coming back to the cases before us, we find that the High Court had correctly stated the grounds on which even a subjective opinion as to the existence of the need to take action under Section 17(4) of the Act can be challenged on certain limited grounds.
But, as soon as we speak of a challenge we have to bear in mind the general burdens laid down by Sections 101 and 102 of the Evidence Act.
It is for the petitioner to substantiate the grounds of his challenge.
This means that the petitioner has to either lead evidence or show that some evidence has come from the side of the respondents to indicate that his challenge to a notification or order is made good.
If he does not succeed in discharging that duty his petition will fail.

30. In the cases before us, if the total evidence from whichever side any of it may have come, was insufficient to enable the petitioners to discharge their general or stable onus, their petitions could not succeed.

On the other hand, if, in addition to the bare assertions made by the petitioners, that the urgency contemplated by Section 17(4)

5 did not exist

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: , there were other facts and circumstances, including the failure of the State to indicate facts and circumstances which it could have easily disclosed if they existed, the petitioners could be held to have discharged their general onus.
40. In the case before us, the public purpose indicated is the development of an area for industrial and residential purposes.

This, in - 10 - itself, on the face of it, does not call for any such action, barring exceptional circumstances, as to make immediate possession, without holding even a summary enquiry under Section 5-A of the Act, imperative.

On the other hand, such schemes generally take sufficient period of time to enable at least summary inquiries under Section 5-A of the Act to be completed without any impediment whatsoever to the execution of the scheme.

Therefore, the very statement of the public purpose for which the land was to be acquired indicated the absence of such urgency, on the apparent facts of the case, as to require the elimination of an enquiry under Section 5-A of the Act.
42. All schemes relating to development of industrial and residential areas must be urgent in the context of the country's need for increased production and more residential accommodation.
Yet, the very nature of such schemes of development does not appear to demand such emergent action as to eliminate summary enquiries under Section 5-A of the Act.

There is no indication whatsoever in the affidavit filed on behalf of the State that the mind of the Commissioner was applied at all to the question whether it was a case necessitating the elimination of the enquiry under Section 5-A of the Act.

The recitals in the notifications, on the other hand, indicate that elimination of the enquiry under Section 5- A of the Act was treated as an automatic consequence of the opinion formed on other matters.
The recital does not say at all that any opinion was formed on the need to dispense with the enquiry under Section 5- A of the Act.
It is certainly a ease in which the recital was at least defective.

The burden, therefore, rested upon the State to remove the defect, if possible, by evidence to show that some exceptional circumstances which necessitated the elimination of an enquiry under Section 5-A of the Act and that the mind of the Commissioner was applied to this essential question.

It seems to us that the High Court correctly applied the provisions of Section 106 of the Evidence Act to place the burden upon the State to prove those special circumstances, although it also appears to us that the High Court was not quite correct - 11 - in stating its view in such a manner as to make it appear that some part of the initial burden of the petitioners under Sections 101 and 102 of the Evidence Act had been displaced by the failure of the State to discharge its duty under Section 106 of the Act.

In the case of The Town Panchayat, Koratagere Town Vs. Sri Krishnappa (supra), this Court has held as under:
"14.

sentences.text: We have perused the record.
Admittedly, in the instant case, the collector has not tendered 80% of the amount of compensation before taking the possession of the land in question i.e., on or before 09.11.2006.

Therefore, in view of the law laid down by three-judge bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in DELHI AIRTECH SERVICES PRIVATE LIMITED (SUPRA), the provisions of Section 11A of the Act apply to the fact situation of the case.
The notification in respect of acquisition of land measuring 3.03 acres has been issued on 09.12.2004.
The final notification was issued on 16.02.2006 and the award was passed beyond a period of 2 years i.e., on 21.06.2008.

Therefore, the learned Single Judge has rightly concluded that the proceedings in respect of land measuring 3.03 acres of survey number 64 situated at Koratagere Town Kasaba, Tumkur District have lapsed under Section 11 of the Act.
As far as the dispute pertaining to 7 acres of land of Sy.No.64 is concerned.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in 'HAMID ALI KHAN (D) THROUGH LRS AND ANOTHER VS. STATE OF U.P. AND OTHERS', (2021) SCC ONLINE SC 1115 referred to with approval the principles laid down in Radhy Shyam's case supra has - 12 - dealt with the scope and ambit of the exercise of powers under Section 17 of the Act.

entities.text: HAMID ALI KHAN (D) THROUGH LRS AND ANOTHER VS. STATE OF U.P. AND OTHERS', (2021) SCC ONLINE SC 1115
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Para 77 of the decision rendered Radhy Shyam's case supra reads as under:
77.

From the analysis of the relevant statutory provisions and interpretation thereof by this Court in different cases, the following principles can be culled out:
(i) Eminent domain is a right inherent in every sovereign to take and appropriate property belonging to citizens for public use.

To put it differently, the sovereign is entitled to reassert its dominion over any portion of the soil of the State including private property without its owner's consent provided that such assertion is on account of public exigency and for public good.

- Dwarkadas Shrinivas v. Sholapur Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd., AIR (1954) SC 119, Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India AIR (1951) SC 41 and Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat (1995)
Supp. (1) SCC 596.

(ii) The legislations which provide for compulsory acquisition of private property by the State fall in the category of expropriatory legislation and such legislation must be construed strictly - DLF Qutab Enclave Complex Educational Charitable Trust v.
State of Haryana (2003) 5 SCC 622; State of Maharashtra v. B.E. Billimoria (2003) 7 SCC 336 and Dev Sharan v. State of U.P., Civil Appeal No.2334 of 2011 decided on 7.3.2011.

State of Haryana (2003) 5 SCC 622

sentences.text: (iii) Though, in exercise of the power of eminent domain, the Government can acquire the private property for public purpose, it must be remembered that compulsory taking of one's property is a serious matter.

If the property belongs to economically disadvantaged segment of the society or people suffering from other handicaps, then the Court is not only entitled but is duty bound to scrutinize the action/decision of the State with greater - 13 - vigilance, care and circumspection keeping in view the fact that the land owner is likely to become landless and deprived of the only source of his livelihood and/or shelter.
(iv) The property of a citizen cannot be acquired by the State and/or its agencies/instrumentalities without complying with the mandate of Sections 4, 5-A and 6 of the Act.

A public purpose, however,
laudable it may be does not entitle the State to invoke the urgency provisions because the same have the effect of depriving the owner of his right to property without being heard.
Only in a case of real urgency, the State can invoke the urgency provisions and dispense with the requirement of hearing the land owner or other interested persons.
(v) Section 17(1) read with Section 17(4) confers extraordinary power upon the State to acquire private property without complying with the mandate of Section 5-A.
These provisions can be invoked only when the purpose of acquisition cannot brook the delay of even few weeks or months.

Therefore, before excluding the application of Section 5-A, the concerned authority must be fully satisfied that time of few weeks or months likely to be taken in conducting inquiry under Section 5-A will, in all probability, frustrate the public purpose for which land is proposed to be acquired.

(vi) The satisfaction of the Government on the issue of urgency is subjective but is a condition precedent to the exercise of power under Section 17(1) and the same can be challenged on the ground that the purpose for which the private property is sought to be acquired is not a public purpose at all or that the exercise of power is vitiated due to mala fides or that the concerned authorities did not apply mind to the relevant factors and the records.

(vii) The exercise of power by the Government under Section 17(1) does not necessarily result in exclusion of Section 5- A of the Act in terms of which any person interested in land can file objection and is entitled to be heard in support of his objection.

The use of word "may" in sub- section (4) of Girish S/O Rajshekhar Kanthi vs State Of Karnataka on 14 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/185926136/
8 Section 17 makes it clear that it merely enables the Government to direct that the provisions of Section 5-A would not apply to the cases covered under sub- section (1) or (2) of Section 17.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In other words, invoking of Section 17(4) is not a necessary concomitant of the exercise of power under Section 17(1).

(viii) The acquisition of land for residential, commercial, industrial or institutional purposes can be treated as an acquisition for public purposes within the meaning of Section 4 but that, by itself, does not justify the exercise of power by the Government under Section 17(1) and/or 17(4).

The Court can take judicial notice of the fact that planning, execution and implementation of the schemes relating to development of residential, commercial, industrial or institutional areas usually take few years.
Therefore, the private property cannot be acquired for such purpose by invoking the urgency provision contained in Section 17(1).
In any case, exclusion of the rule of audi alteram partem embodied in Section 5-A (1) and (2) is not at all warranted in such matters.

(ix) If land is acquired for the benefit of private persons, the Court should view the invoking of Section 17(1) and/or 17(4) with suspicion and carefully scrutinize the relevant record before adjudicating upon the legality of such acquisition.
15. In the instant case, the notification under Section 4(1) read with Section 17(1) of the Act was issued on 09.12.2004.
If there was - 15 - really an urgency in acquisition of the land, the appellant ought to have acted with quite promptitude.

However, final notification under Section 6 of the Act was issued after a period of 14 months on 16.02.2006 and thereafter, nearly after a period of approximately 9 months, the possession of the land in question was taken.

Therefore, it is evident that there was no urgency in acquisition of the land in question and the State Government was not justified in invoking the urgency provision as contained in Section 17(1) of the Act.
16. Thus, it can safely be inferred that right of the respondent to a hearing under Section 5A of the Act has been taken away without any justifiable reason.
Even otherwise, learned counsel for the appellant has stated that appellant does not require the aforesaid land.
17. Learned counsel for the appellant has submitted that since, the appellant has utilised the land in question, therefore, the relief is be moulded in facts of the case.
From perusal of the photographs annexed with the petition, we find that the appellant has only constructed a boundary wall and has dumped garbage on the land in question.
Therefore, the land in question measuring 3.03 acres remains an open land.

Therefore, the question of moulding the relief and permitting the appellant to retain the possession of the land in question does not arise as the respondents cannot be deprived of their constituted right under Article 300A of the Constitution of India.

In view of preceding analysis we do not find any merit in this appeal the same fails and is here by dismissed."

sentences.text:
As can be seen from the aforesaid judgments, invocation of urgency clause u/S 17 is permissible only if there exists extreme and genuine or compelling urgency for use of land for public purpose and in the absence of sufficient or valid reasons/ urgency,
- 16 - it cannot be said that the respondents are entitled to invoke Sec.17 thereby depriving a land owner of his valuable constitutional right envisaged under Article 300-A of the Constitution of India.

In the facts of the instant case, I am of the considered opinion that the material on record neither warranted nor justified invocation of the urgency clause contemplated u/S 17 of the L.A. Act and consequently, the impugned preliminary notification deserves to be quashed.

9. The material on record also discloses that despite the petitioner filing a detailed objections along with documents to the preliminary notification explaining the earlier Court proceedings which culminated in favour of the petitioner pursuant to which the second respondent - Deputy Commissioner, directed the third respondent-SLAO/ Assistant Commissioner to consider the same,
the respondents have proceeded to issue the impugned final notification without considering the said objections, documents or circumstances and without providing any opportunity to the petitioners or hearing them and consequently, the impugned final notification is violative of principles of natural justice and the same deserves to be quashed.
- 17 - 10.

It is also relevant to state that the chronology of events prior to the impugned preliminary notification make it unmistakably clear that the impugned acquisition proceedings are a result of malafides, colourable exercise of power as well as fraud on power in as much as the 4th respondent-APMC for whose benefit the subject lands are notified, had litigated right upto the Apex Court and after having lost the said litigations to the petitioners, the instant acquisition proceedings are a clear subterfuge and an attempt to circumvent the earlier rounds of litigation wherein the 4th respondent was unsuccessful thereby establishing that the impugned acquisition proceedings are tainted with malafides and are in bad faith and deserve to be quashed as held by this Court in the case of Hanumegouda vs. State of Karnatka & others (2004 AIR-KANT.H.C.R.1408).
11.

In the light of the aforesaid judgment of this Court and the undisputed facts obtaining in the instant case, preceding the impugned preliminary notification, I am of the considered opinion that the impugned acquisition proceedings are vitiated by bad faith, malafides and colourable exercise of power and the same deserve to be quashed on this ground also.
- 18 - 12.
In the result, I pass the following order.

opennyai_summary.facts: It is the grievance of the petitioner that despite all the aforesaid proceedings which have attained finality and become conclusive in favour of the petitioner, the respondents No.1 to 3 have colluded with each other and fraudulently issued the impugned preliminary notification dated 21.12.2009 under Sec. 4(1) of the L.A. Act illegally purporting to invoke the urgency provisions of Sec. 17 of the L.A. Act thereby dispensing with the mandatory enquiry provided under Sec. 5-A of the L.A. Act and despite the petitioners filing their objections on 01.02.2010 along with all relevant documents including the aforesaid Court proceedings and orders pursuant to which the second respondent addressed a communication dated 04.02.2010 directing the third respondent- LAO to consider the said objections and documents of the petitioners, the respondents have proceeded to issue the impugned final notification dated 24.05.2010 which is an outcome of bad faith, malafides and colourable exercise of power and the same deserves to be quashed.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In this context, a perusal of the preliminary notification dated 21.12.2009 will clearly indicate that the only property sought to be acquired under the said notification was the subject land of the petitioners by invoking Sec. 17 of the L.A. Act and mandatory enquiry under Section 5-A of the L.A. Act was sought to be dispensed with by the respondents;
however, neither the said notification nor any other material placed by the respondents establish the urgency or the exceptional/ extra ordinary circumstances which warranted invocation of the urgency clause contained in Sec.17 thereby dispensing with the mandatory enquiry contemplated u/S 5-A of the L.A. Act; in fact, except for stating that the subject lands were required for the purpose of 4th respondent-APMC, neither valid nor justifiable reasons are assigned either in the preliminary notification nor in any other document by the respondents to justify invocation of Sec.17 and consequently, the very invocation of Sec. 17 by the respondents is illegal and contrary to the law laid down by the Apex Court and this Court in the following judgments, i.e., (i) Hamid Ali Khan Vs. State of U.P. & Others (2021 SCC Online SC 1115) and (ii) The Town Panchayat, Koratagere Girish S/O Rajshekhar Kanthi vs State Of Karnataka on 14 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/185926136/
Therefore, the very statement of the public purpose for which the land was to be acquired indicated the absence of such urgency, on the apparent facts of the case, as to require the elimination of an enquiry under Section 5-A of the Act.
42. All schemes relating to development of industrial and residential areas must be urgent in the context of the country's need for increased production and more residential accommodation.
Yet, the very nature of such schemes of development does not appear to demand such emergent action as to eliminate summary enquiries under Section 5-A of the Act.

If the property belongs to economically disadvantaged segment of the society or people suffering from other handicaps, then the Court is not only entitled but is duty bound to scrutinize the action/decision of the State with greater - 13 - vigilance, care and circumspection keeping in view the fact that the land owner is likely to become landless and deprived of the only source of his livelihood and/or shelter.
Only in a case of real urgency, the State can invoke the urgency provisions and dispense with the requirement of hearing the land owner or other interested persons.
(ix) If land is acquired for the benefit of private persons, the Court should view the invoking of Section 17(1) and/or 17(4) with suspicion and carefully scrutinize the relevant record before adjudicating upon the legality of such acquisition.
15. In the instant case, the notification under Section 4(1) read with Section 17(1) of the Act was issued on 09.12.2004.
If there was - 15 - really an urgency in acquisition of the land, the appellant ought to have acted with quite promptitude.
However, final notification under Section 6 of the Act was issued after a period of 14 months on 16.02.2006 and thereafter, nearly after a period of approximately 9 months, the possession of the land in question was taken.
Therefore, it is evident that there was no urgency in acquisition of the land in question and the State Government was not justified in invoking the urgency provision as contained in Section 17(1) of the Act.
Therefore, the question of moulding the relief and permitting the appellant to retain the possession of the land in question does not arise as the respondents cannot be deprived of their constituted right under Article 300A of the Constitution of India.
As can be seen from the aforesaid judgments, invocation of urgency clause u/S 17 is permissible only if there exists extreme and genuine or compelling urgency for use of land for public purpose and in the absence of sufficient or valid reasons/ urgency,
- 16 - it cannot be said that the respondents are entitled to invoke Sec.17 thereby depriving a land owner of his valuable constitutional right envisaged under Article 300-A of the Constitution of India.
In the facts of the instant case, I am of the considered opinion that the material on record neither warranted nor justified invocation of the urgency clause contemplated u/S 17 of the L.A. Act and consequently, the impugned preliminary notification deserves to be quashed.
